description: This dataset label combines two related but distinct entities: Actinic Keratosis (AK), a precancerous scaly skin growth caused by cumulative UV damage that may be an early form of squamous cell carcinoma, and Bowen's disease (intraepidermal/intraepithelial squamous cell carcinoma), a noninvasive, full-thickness carcinoma in situ sometimes called 'stage 0' skin cancer. Both arise on sun-damaged skin and exist on a spectrum toward invasive squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
taxonomy_note: AKIEC is a combined dataset category, not a single clinical diagnosis. Actinic keratosis (lower, variable per-lesion progression risk) and Bowen's disease (already an in-situ carcinoma, historically staged separately) are clinically distinct and are conflated under this single label. A prediction of 'AKIEC' cannot by itself indicate which of the two is present; this entry documents both.
symptoms: Actinic keratosis: rough, dry, scaly, or sandpaper-like patch, often felt before it is seen
Actinic keratosis: flat to slightly raised patch, typically under 1-2 cm, colored red, pink, tan, brown, skin-colored, gray, yellow, white, or silvery
Actinic keratosis: may itch, burn, sting, feel tender, bleed, or catch on clothing; occasionally a horn-like growth
Actinic keratosis: common on sun-exposed skin - face, lips, ears, scalp, neck, shoulders, back of hands/forearms, lower legs
Bowen's disease: persistent reddish-brown or orange-red, scaly, flat or slightly raised patch or plaque
Bowen's disease: most lesions are asymptomatic; some itch, ooze, bleed, crust, or feel tender
Bowen's disease: most common on sun-exposed skin, especially the lower legs; can also occur on ears, face, hands, genitals, or in the mouth
warning_signs: Actinic keratosis becoming tender, thickened, ulcerated, or enlarging - suspicious for evolution to invasive SCC
A horn-shaped actinic keratosis, which may indicate higher risk
Bowen's disease developing a fleshy nodule or bump within the lesion
Bowen's disease becoming tender or bleeding easily
Bowen's disease showing ulceration or hardening (induration) - described as early indicators of malignant transformation
recommendation: See a board-certified dermatologist for evaluation of any new or changing scaly patch. Reported treatment options include cryotherapy, curettage, excision, topical therapies (5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, diclofenac), and photodynamic therapy; a single stable actinic keratosis may sometimes be monitored without immediate treatment. Sun protection is recommended for prevention.
